Kriging Empirical Mode Decomposition via support vector machine learning
technique for autonomous operation diagnosing of CHP in microgrid
Zehui Shao a,⁎
, Karzan Wakil b,c, Muhammet Usak d, Mohammad Amin Heidari e, Bo Wang f,
Rolando Simoes g

HIGHLIGHTS
•Negligible none detection zone for CHP generator.
•Avoiding of threshold selection.
•Suitable for microgrid application.
•Usable in noisy condition.
•Best data selection method.
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
CHP
Islanding detection
Empirical mode decomposition
Pattern learning
Optimal support vector machine
Signal selection
ABSTRACT
Combined Heat and Power (CHP) is the one of new energy resources which has been added to power system in
recent years. High eﬃciency, Loss reducing of power system and etc, are the main advantages of CHP as same as
other distributed generations. But, unwanted islanding is one of the main problems for this generation. This
article presents a novel technique for CHP unit islanding detection using Kriging Empirical Mode Decomposition
(KEMD) and Support Vector Machine (SVM) pattern learning technique. In this technique the variation of
Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMF) of local signals in two-dimensional mode is utilized as input data of relay. An
optimal signal selection model is applied to the proposed relay in order to Non-Detection Zone (NDZ) and fails
detection reducing. The best signal selection is introduces based on mean square value between islanding and
non-islanding conditions. Also, by considering Optimal SVM model for the proposed relay as a pattern re-
cognizing and weighing it using shark smell optimization, this technique has overcome the threshold selection
problem. This relay is applied to CHP system in a microgrid system contains various types of DGs. Many is-
landing and non-islanding situation in various operation conditions in the studied microgrid are simulated. The
results of simulation results are show that the proposed relay is suitable for microgrid application. Negligible
NDZ, high detection time, zero fail detection and low cost of this relay are the main advantages of the proposed
technique.
1. Introduction
With the increasing energy consumption, environmental carbon
release and depletion of fossil fuels, Energy manufacturers tend to in-
crease the use of renewable energy such as wind power, solar
photovoltaic and land ﬁll gas [1]. Individual Distributed Generation
(DG) connected to the power system has intermittence, randomness and
the uncertainty character, which are di ﬃ cult to troubleshoot in some
cases in power systems [2]. In order to solve these problems, some
solutions are suggested in microgrid [3]. The microgrid is a subsystem

of power system that consists of multiple DG units, storage devices and
loads which that can be activated in both grid-connected and islanded
(autonomous) modes [4]. If all or part of the microgrid, including load
and DG, is separated from the main grid and DGs remain, the island
state has occurred [5].
Islanding conditions are being planned or undesirable [6]. In the
planned islanding conditions, it is possible to provide active/reactive
power for MG loads using by DG units and there is no active/reactive
power interchange with the grid. As a result, island conditions operate
without any transients, and the MG continues performing like an in-
dependent system [7]. In some cases, island conditions occur because of
disturbances in the system. If the unwanted island conditions do not
occur, the operating conditions of the MG depend on the delivery of
electrical loads between DG units or importing or exporting energy
from/to the grid can be altered. These conditions must be identi ﬁed in
order to control the sources of MG, when island conditions occur.
In general, in order to identify unwanted island conditions, there are
three possible solutions: passive, active and remote techniques [8]. The
process of Remote operation [9] is based on the relationship between
the utility and the DGs. The disadvantages of this method are high costs
and the di ﬃ culty of implementing it. An active method cause dis-
turbances in distributed systems and pushes the system in an island
state towards unstable [10]. Because of the disadvantages of these
methods and their performance in both grid-connected and autono-
mous conditions, both techniques are inappropriate for microgrid re-
sources. Therefore, the mentioned methods are not useful for distribu-
tion systems [11].
The active method is proportional with the parameters of the power
system (voltage, current, frequency and etc) and identi ﬁes the island
mode using data processing. The active method is proportional with the
parameters of the power system and identi ﬁes the island mode using
data processing. A number of active techniques are: over/under voltage
(OV/UV) and frequency (OF/UF) [12], total harmonic distortions [13],
rate of change of frequency and rate of change of generator power
output [14], phase displacement monitoring, vector surge [15], rate of
change of phase angle derivation [16], absolute value of certain wa-
velet coe ﬃ cient [17],Time-frequency detection algorithm [18], tran-
sient current and voltage signals through discrete wavelet transform
[19,20]. It should be noted that the unwanted island state occurring in
power balance operation, some passive islanding discovery approaches
may not respond properly, or it takes a long time to identify the islands.
Also, one of the most important issues in the passive technique is the
choice of threshold. Too low values of the threshold cause the nuisance
tripping problem, and on the contrary, the high value of the threshold
islanding may not be identify.
Recently, islanding diagnosing technique using wavelets models are
widely applied to distributed generations for develop the performance
of passive methods. Stability, ﬂexibility, Simplicity and low cost to
implementation are the main advantages of WT methods. some of WT
methods are; WGM1.0 & Machine learning [21], WSE & matrix analysis
[22], Haar & Neuro-Fuzzy [23], Daubechies db4 [24], WPT & dq frame
analysis [25],
Wavelet singular entropy [26]. In the mentioned
methods, the signal selection method hasn ’ t applied to detection pro-
cess. Also, in the above methods the value of signal is considered which
can be caused to mistake detection. Moreover, another main problem in
passive algorithms is the choosing of the threshold. If this threshold be
very low the wrong tripping makes challenge, otherwise with very high
values of threshold, detection of islanding mode may not be done.
In this paper, the various local signals are measured in the Power
Common Coupling (PCC) point of DG and these signals are sorted by a
mathematical theory and the best of them is selected as input signal. At
First, all of local signals are recorded under various islanding and non-
islanding situation under every loading conditions of network. In next
step, using Kriging Empirical Mode Decomposition (KEMD) in various
decomposition levels, measured signals' are decomposed. Two criter-
ions named islanding signals' standard deviation (ISSD) and cross is-
landing and non-islanding signal's standard deviation (CINSSD) are
deﬁned for optimal signal selection and all of signals are sorted using
these criterions. The SVM based technique is designed for state varia-
tion of this signal and the relay is trained optimally using optimization
algorithms and these signals are employed as input data. Totally, the
proposed method has prominent features as bellow:
•Optimal signal selecting using two deﬁ ned ISSD and CINSSD cri-
terions.
•Choosing optimum window time and number of signals as input for
relay.
•Negligible non-detection zone achievement and signi ﬁcant reduc-
tion noise sensitivity.
•Avoidance from de ﬁning threshold value by considering SVM.
The proposed technique is applied to CHP unit in study microgrid

2. System description
The studied system in this paper is a microgrid contains various
distributed generation with a state space mathematical model and NDZ
opinion and formulation. With the aim of describing the function of the
target algorithm in the NDZ regions, the size of decomposition pro-
cessing window and the method of island identi ﬁcation are formulated.

2.3. Prescribed events
The suggested approach for identifying the island is obtained by
analyzing the frequency time-frequency and learning in a stable vari-
able. Some of the events are distinct according to the operational re-
quirements in IEEE1547 standards and possible operating network to
choice the appropriate variables and learn the proposed relay. In order
to maintain the main characteristics of the system performance, events
are simulated o ﬀ-line, which is presented in the proposed method. In
general, events are classi ﬁed into two categories include: namely is-
landing and non-islanding, which are taken for the proposed islanding
detection relays.
In small imbalance active and reactive power situations (NDZ), BR2,
BR4, and BR7 are unlocked.
(a) In large imbalance active and reactive power, BR2 and BR7 are
unlocked.
(b) Tripping breakers BR7, BR8, and BR9 subsequent to a high re-
sistance fault at bus B5,
(c) Tripping breakers ‘ BR2’ and ‘ BR4’ subsequent to a high resistance
fault at bus B2.
Events for non-islanding conditions are expressed as follows.
(a) Motor operating with di ﬀerent capacities at buses B5 and B1
(b) at buses B5 and B1, Capacitor bank switching with di ﬀerent capa-
cities,
(c) Non-linear load connecting to network at buses B5 and B1,
(d) Tripping BR3 and disconnecting DG1,
In accordance with the number of functional loads and di ﬀerent
settings of the testing system, consist of radial/ring structure of mi-
crogrid, all of the cases mentioned above are simulated. A total of 744
events have been simulated, of which 524 are island condition and 350
cases are related to match power conditions (NDZ), and 174 cases are
associated to mismatch power conditions. Similarly, the non-island
mode is also simulated on 220 cases.

EMD utilizes a repetitive sifting procedure for parsing signal to IM
function elements. Steps of this process can be brie ﬂy described as

EMD algorithm:
(1) Compute the local maximum and minimum of the signal, indicated
by x(t), within the assumed domain.
(2) Connect the maximum of x(t) with an interpolating function, such
as to an upper envelope u(t)is generated around the signal. EMD
utilizes spline of third-order, known as Cubic Spline (CS), for the
interpolation [27]. Likely, connect the minimum of x(t) with the
interpolating function to generated a lower envelope l(t) about the
signal. Fig. 4 illustrated these envelopes.
(3) The upper and lower envelopes average, i.e., s(t)=[ u(t)+ l(t)]/2,
is computed, which is the curve of local average in Fig. 1.
(4) If the stopping condition a is contented, the local average s(t)i sa n
IMF and go to step 5; otherwise, replace the signal with signal
minus the local average, i.e., x(t) − s(t) → x(t), and go back to step
2.

1(t), s2(t), … , sn(t) have been created so
far. Calculate the residual r(t)= x(t) − [s1(t)+ s2(t)+ … + sn(t)].
If the stopping condition b is contented, terminate the algorithm;
otherwise, replace the signal with the residual, i.e., r(t) → x(t), and
go back to step 2.
Stop term states, the comparative variance among 2 consecutive

random function, allocates weights based on data driven method which
leads to upper weights to insulated points contrasting to points in a
cluster. Furthermore, this method in addition to parameter estimation
can estimate also its error via kriging variance [31].

4. Proposed detection method
If active methods are used to identify the island conditions of DGs in
the microgrid system, the microgrid system becomes unstable in island
conditions. So, for all DGs in microgrid, the active method is not a good
option. In available passive methods, island conditions are identi ﬁed by

and saved all events. These variables are sorted by their type and re-
lation. These parameters are formulated according to the equations as

4.4. Stricture of proposed relay
Fig. 10 shows the structure of the proposed relay for CHP generator
islanding detection. This technique uses rate of change of active and
reactive power at the Power Common Coupling (PCC) point of CHP in
study microgrid system. As can be seen in Fig. 10, in the next step, the
variation of IMF 2 coeﬃ cient of KEMD for the inputs distributed gen-
erations is calculated. Using active and reactive signals, the value of
IMF2 variation of KEMD signals for these parameters are calculated (see
Fig. 10). These values variation of KEMD coe ﬃ cients are fed to the SVM
for training and detecting the islanding conditions. If the islanding is
detected, outputs of the proposed relay will be 1; otherwise, the is-
landing is not detected and the output will be 0. Using SVM system the
proposed technique can overcome the problem of setting the detection
thresholds inherent in the existing techniques.
The proposed relay training is one of the other important parts of
the proposed relay. The number of input data and number of events
data for training are two major factors that a ﬀects on the proposed
relay performance.
- Number of input data ( NID): The number of relay input data depends
on the time interval for feeding of selected signal. As can be seen in
Fig. 2, the transient time of the system is 0.2 s which is selected for
the proposed method.
- Number of events for training ( NEV): another factor a ﬀecting the
relay's performance is the number of island and non-island condition
events for relay training. In the proposed method, number of events
has changed between 10 and 90 percent of total data by steps of 5
percent.
In order to achieve the optimal condition, the number of input data
and the number of event for training is selected by considering Receiver
Operating Characteristic (ROC) and Area under the curve (AUC) [37].
One of the most appropriate criterions to appraising the e ﬃ ciency of
classiﬁers is the ROC. Some of utilities of this curve are speci ﬁcation of
proper operational condition of a certain classi ﬁer and indicating the
most appropriate classiﬁer through several of them. Number of true and
false categorizations is the output of a classi ﬁer [37]. Here in order to
determine the number of input data and number of events for relay
training, the training data process is utilized. After signal selection
